I found relevant information about Ghostty terminal's tab title functionality and escape sequences. Here's what I discovered:

## Tab Title Configuration

Window and tab titles can now be set separately from split titles using the menu, command palette, or new keybind actions, which was added in version 1.3.0.

You can change the title of the current tab via a pop-up prompt, where the title set via this prompt overrides any title set by the terminal and persists across focus changes within the tab. Additionally, you can set the title for the current focused tab using keybind actions, and if the title is empty, the tab title override is cleared.

## Title Configuration Option

Regarding the `title` configuration option, if it is unset, the next title change escape sequence will be honored but previous changes will not retroactively be set, which may require you to restart programs such as Neovim to get the new title.

## OSC Escape Sequences

OSC sequences are typically used to encode strings or other non-integer data to transmit between the terminal and an application, and they usually alter variables regarding the terminal emulator itself, such as its title, palette, clipboard, etc.

The search results show that Ghostty supports OSC title escape sequences, though there was a historical issue reported (issue #1026) where OSC 1 sequences weren't working for setting tab titles, but this appears to have been addressed in later versions.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

content.text:
Yes, it's possible — but it's a shell-side trick, not a built-in Ghostty feature. Here's the picture:

## What Ghostty gives you

- Ghostty honors the standard **OSC title escape sequences** (`OSC 0` = icon+window title, `OSC 2` = window title — the tab label follows these). So anything that prints those sequences can set the tab title live.
- **Caveat:** if you've set a fixed `title = ...` in your Ghostty config, that *overrides* and suppresses programmatic title changes. Leave `title` unset for this to work.
- There's **no built-in "last activity timestamp"** anywhere in Ghostty itself — it only renders whatever title sequence it last received.

So the trick is: have your shell emit an OSC-2 sequence containing a timestamp whenever a command runs.

## The recipe (zsh — you're on zsh)

Add to `~/.zshrc`:

```zsh
autoload -Uz add-zsh-hook

# Fires right before each prompt is drawn — i.e. just after the last command finished
_ghostty_title() {
  print -Pn "\e]2;${PWD:t} · $(date +%H:%M)\a"
}
add-zsh-hook precmd _ghostty_title
```

That gives a tab title like `cli · 14:32`, where the time updates to when the last command **finished**. If you'd rather stamp when a command **starts**, use `preexec` instead of `precmd`.

## The one real limitation

The title only updates **when the shell hook fires** — i.e. at prompt time. So:

- "Last change" effectively means "last command boundary," not "last byte of output." A long-running command that keeps printing won't bump the timestamp until it returns.
- If you want it to reflect output activity *during* a long command, you'd need that command to emit its own OSC-2 sequences (some tools do), or a more involved wrapper — there's no terminal-level hook for "screen content changed."

If by "change" you actually meant something else (a file edit in the repo, a checkpoint, etc.), tell me and I'll adjust the trigger — the title-setting mechanism is the same, only what fires it changes.

- [Ghostty 1.3.0 release notes (tab title actions)](https://ghostty.org/docs/install/release-notes/1-3-0)

Nice find — that's a much better approach than the `Stop` hook. Here's the comment (by `sswthrower`, 2026-02-21):

> **Workaround using statusLine** — set the terminal title as a side effect of the `statusLine` command by writing the OSC escape directly to `/dev/tty`, bypassing stdout so it doesn't interfere with the status bar:
> ```bash
> printf "\033]0;%s\007" "$title" > /dev/tty 2>/dev/null
> ```
> Build `$title` from whatever the status line JSON gives you and drop it in before the final `printf "%b" "$result"`.

**Why this beats the Stop hook:** the `statusLine` command runs on *every render* — the same moments Claude repaints the title. So its title write coincides with (and overrides) Claude's own, which is exactly the focused-window race we couldn't win from a `Stop` hook. And you already have a statusLine script, so it folds right in.

Two adaptations for your setup:
1. `/dev/tty` failed for us earlier on macOS (no controlling terminal in the spawned process), so I'll reuse the `$PPID`→`/dev/ttysNNN` resolution that we proved works.
2. statusLine re-renders on activity and freezes when idle — so stamping the *current* time each render naturally gives you "time of last change" (it stops advancing when Claude goes quiet).

# --- Ghostty tab title: stamp dir + last-activity time ---
# statusLine runs on each render, so writing the title here wins the repaint
# race against Claude Code's own title updates, even on the focused window.
# /dev/tty fails in this spawned context on macOS, so resolve Claude's tty via $PPID.
tab_tty=$(ps -o tty= -p "$PPID" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
if [ -n "$tab_tty" ] && [ "$tab_tty" != "??" ]; then
    printf '\033]0;%s · %s\007' "${cwd##*/}" "$(date +%H:%M)" > "/dev/$tab_tty" 2>/dev/null

input.new_string:
# --- Ghostty tab title: "HH:MM - dir - PR #.. T #.." (last-activity time) ---
# Claude's own title updates are off (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE=1), so
# this statusLine side-effect is the sole title writer. /dev/tty fails in this
# spawned context on macOS, so resolve Claude's controlling tty via $PPID.
tab_tty=$(ps -o tty= -p "$PPID" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
if [ -n "$tab_tty" ] && [ "$tab_tty" != "??" ]; then
    # PR + trail lookups hit the network, so cache per-branch and refresh in the
    # background when older than 60s — keeps the status line render fast.
    title_extra=""
    branch=$(git -C "$cwd" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>/dev/null)
    if [ -n "$branch" ]; then
        cache_dir="/tmp/claude-title-cache"
        mkdir -p "$cache_dir"
        cache_file="$cache_dir/$(echo "$branch" | tr '/ ' '__')"
        if [ ! -f "$cache_file" ] || [ -n "$(find "$cache_file" -mmin +1 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
            touch "$cache_file"  # claim it so concurrent renders don't all refresh
            (
                pr=$(cd "$cwd" && gh pr view --json number --jq '.number' 2>/dev/null)
                trail=$(cd "$cwd" && entire trail show 2>/dev/null | awk '/Number:/{print $2; exit}')
                out=""
                [ -n "$pr" ] && out="PR #$pr"
                [ -n "$trail" ] && out="${out:+$out }T #$trail"
                printf '%s' "$out" > "$cache_file"
            ) >/dev/null 2>&1 &
        fi
        title_extra=$(cat "$cache_file" 2>/dev/null)
    fi
    tab_time=$(date +%H:%M)
    tab_dir="${cwd##*/}"
    if [ -n "$title_extra" ]; then
        tab_title="$tab_time - $tab_dir - $title_extra"
    else
        tab_title="$tab_time - $tab_dir"
    fi
    printf '\033]0;%s\007' "$tab_title" > "/dev/$tab_tty" 2>/dev/null
fi

How it behaves:
- **Format:** `HH:MM - <dir> - PR #… T #…`. If there's no open PR or no trail for the branch, that piece is simply omitted (e.g. just `15:55 - cli - T #707`, or `15:55 - cli` on a branch with neither).
- **Fast:** `gh` and `entire trail show` only run in a **background refresh** at most once every 60s per branch, cached in `/tmp/claude-title-cache/`. Renders just read the cache file, so the status bar never blocks on network.
- **First render on a new branch:** the PR/trail part may be blank for ~1 render (a second or two) while the cache fills, then it appears.
- Same as before: the time freezes at last activity when Claude goes idle = your "last change" marker.

If you'd rather show only the PR *or* only the trail, or want a different separator (e.g. `PR #1581 · T #707`), say so and I'll tweak the format.
